text.front:
Picturing Africa and documenting war:
soldiers' photographs from East Africa,
1914-19
DANIEL STEINBACH
University of Copenhagen, Copenhagen, Denmark
During First World War, thousands of British soldiers were sent to fight in
German East Africa, often unaware of their deployment until en route.
Many brought cameras, capturing images of African landscapes, people,
and wildlife. Their unprepared encounter offers unique insights into
British perceptions of colonial Africa. Their photographs, shaped by imper-
ial aesthetics, contrast their role as soldiers in a brutal campaign. This art-
icle examines how their images document both their perceptions of Africa
and the destruction of colonial infrastructure, challenging the myth of the
European 'civilising mission' amid war's devastation.
KEYWORDS Colonialism; photography; First World War; Africa; race
text.body:
On 10 November 1916, The Illustrated London News, a well-established weekly
paper in Britain, published a photographic page under the heading 'The War in
East Africa: Notes on Trek and in Camp'. The photographs assembled on this page
depict a war very different from that portrayed in images from the Western Front,
where the last days of the Battle of the Somme were fought (Figure 1).
In contrast to the suffering, 'senseless' slaughter, and mass death typically associ-
ated with the trenches of France and Flanders, the imagery from East Africa was
consistent with an older imperial aesthetic in which 'gallant' white soldiers fought
an honourable war with the support of colonial troops.
In keeping with this aesthetic, the extra-European theatres of the war, most not-
ably the Allied conquest of the German colonies in Africa, developed a very differ-
ent character from that of the Western Front in the British public imagination, and
in subsequent collective memory. On the periphery, far from the battlelines of
Europe, war was not only an undertaking of the 'united' British Empire, including
colonial forces from Africa and India; it was also an undertaking of order, forward
movement, and military control.

This article examines the photographs taken by white British officers and soldiers
who served in the Allied campaign against German East Africa (modern Tanzania).
Historical photographs are a captivating medium, providing seemingly instant
access to the experiences and impressions of actors from distant times. Yet photo-
graphs are difficult to read and interpret on their own. Instead, these must be 'seen'
FIGURE 1.
The Illustrated London News 148 (4047) 11 November 1916.
text.note: D. STEINBACH
text.body:
and interpreted in the context of wider cultural frameworks, including the aes-
thetic, social and ideological assumptions that shape what is photographed and
how. In keeping with this, my examination of these images places them in the con-
text of letters, diaries, and other writings produced by the same soldiers. Here, both
coherence and discrepancy between image and word become equally revealing
about the assumptions guiding the initial production and subsequent use of photog-
raphy. In the case of war in East Africa, my examination shows how soldiers' selec-
tion of photographs helped to shape their own idea of the war in this particular
place, but also how the imagery they produced heavily influenced the public
imagination and memory of this war. Ultimately, I argue that photographs were an
important tool for developing a narrative that combined colonial expectations with
the pressures of modern war.
Over the last two decades, scholarly work has firmly (re-)established the global
nature of the First World War. A notable feature of this development has been a
widening of perspectives on the war. Whereas attention traditionally focused on the
iconic battlefields of the Western Front, researchers now examine war as it
unfolded in those areas previously relegated to the periphery of both geography
and memory. During the war, armed conflict took place in all regions of the world;
and, as the major belligerents were also colonial powers, foremost Britain and
France, millions of colonial subjects from Africa and Asia were also recruited for
war service in Europe. 1 European men also left Europe to serve in the campaigns
against the Ottoman empire and -on a smaller scale -against the German colonies
in Africa. As such, this period was more than just a battle between European people
and interests; it was also a moment that brought peoples and interests from across
the globe into contact with each other -sometimes in ways that were unique, unex-
pected, or surprising to those involved.
On the African continent, most of the four German colonies were quickly occupied
by the Allies within a couple of months of the outbreak of war. 2 The conquest of
German East Africa, however, became a prolonged campaign that lasted until
November 1918. Originally, Britain had planned to conquer this colony from neigh-
bouring British East Africa (today Kenya) using its professional colonial army, the
King's African Rifles, and the Indian Expeditionary Force C that arrived in the
autumn of 1914. 3 The German colonial army in East Africa, the Schutztruppe, was,
however, able to repel the British attack in the battle of Tanga, turning the war into a
stalemate that lasted for over a year. By spring 1916, Britain had assembled a renewed
force with men from across the East African region, as well as South Africans,
Indians, and British soldiers from Europe. Later, these were joined by men from

2011); Heike Liebau et al., eds, The World in World Wars: Experiences, Perceptions and Perspectives
from Africa and Asian (Leiden/Bosten: Brill, 2010); Timothy C. Winegard, Indigenous Peoples of the
British Dominions and the First World War (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2012).
2 Hew Strachan, The First World War in Africa (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2004).

3 Edward Paice, Tip and Run: The Untold Tragedy of the Great War in Africa (London: Weidenfeld and
Nicolson, 2007); S. D. Pradhan, Indian Army in East Africa, 1914-918 (New Delhi: National Book

Everyday Colonialism in German East Africa (Athens, OH: Ohio University Press, 2014), 115-47.
PICTURING AFRICA AND DOCUMENTING WAR
text.body:
Nigeria, the (then) Gold Coast, and the West Indies. For the next two and a half years,
this imperial army fought slowly, but steadily, against the retreating Schutztruppe.
Although imperial wars fought before 1914 also drew on multi-racial and multi-
ethnic manpower, never before had Britain amassed such a diverse force from across
its empire. 4 This moment of inter-imperial and international encounter exposed
multiple contradictions, which threatened the very idea of colonial power. Here,
white British soldiers fought against another colonising power with the support of
colonial subjects, men whom many would have regarded as racially and culturally
'inferior'; although success was dependent on soldiers and auxiliaries from Africa
and India, this dependency could not be allowed to undermine the imperial order.
This contradiction, and the tensions it created, has been observed to play out in mul-
tiple domains -including issues of 'imperial masculinities', local knowledge, and the
way the conflict was memorialised. 5 Typically, the analyses contained in such work
draw on textual primary sources, such as official documents, newspapers, letters,
diaries, and memoirs. Here I focus on what can be learned about such tensions, how
they were experienced and resolved, through the unique lens of photography.
Although there is a long tradition of discussing the relation between photographs
and modern wars, historians of the First World War have been slow to include
images in their repertoire of primary sources. 6 Given the vast amount of photo-
graphic material produced by official photographers and private soldiers, it is sur-
prising how few studies of this material have been integrated into a wider history of
the war. 7 Partly in response to the centenary of the war, and also in response to pro-
gress with large digitisation projects, however, over recent years the events of 1914-
18 have been revisited and the literature on war photography has also expended
considerably. In relation to the latter, a particular interest has been in non-official
images taken privately by ordinary soldiers (although a precise distinction between
official and non-official imagery is often difficult to uphold). Through these images,
we can begin to grasp how private and semi-public memory was constructed. 8

D. STEINBACH
text.body:
It is noticeable that historians of the colonial dimension of this war have been espe-
cially innovative in utilising these visual sources. As Santanu Das has stressed in his
work on Indian soldiers serving in Europe, images are of particular importance in the
context of men who left only few written traces -without attending to non-textual
sources, the voices of these colonised men can too easily be ignored. 9 Several histori-
ans on the Middle Eastern campaign have also drawn on photographs to develop a
more nuanced understanding of the relations between its participants. 10 These works
show how photographs can fill gaps in officially recorded 'knowledge' and to bridge
gaps between the experience of war and worlds of home and family far away.
Although built on firm foundations, including the established historiography of colo-
nial photography 11 and scholarship on the cultural history of the First World War,
these studies remain exceptions. Daniel Foliard's recent book embeds the photo-
graphic outputs of the war years into a wider imperial visual culture. 12 The general
absence of interest in photographic sources among colonial historians remains pro-
nounced, however, especially in relation to the African campaigns of the war.
Absence of interest is not limited to photographic sources. In the historiography of
colonial Africa, the First World War is an often-overlooked chapter. Yet, during this
period, millions of African civilians were conscripted for the military as soldiers or -
much more often -as porters or labourers, creating an unprecedent movement of peo-
ple. The same period witnessed several anti-colonial insurgencies across the continent,
lasting societal changes, and -in German East Africa -a collapse of the agricultural
economy, leading to famines with several hundred thousand deaths. 13 Despite all the
above, few works dealing with specific African colonies or regions give enough room
to the social and economic upheaval that this war brought to the continent. 14
What can we learn by approaching photography of the First World War in East
Africa from these combined angles of military and colonial history? Many of the

PICTURING AFRICA AND DOCUMENTING WAR
text.body:
photographs we have from this period come from British men deployed to fight in
Africa. These men were a curious group because they were the first Europeans to fight
in colonial Africa without specifically volunteering to be there. Typically, they set sail
from Plymouth or Portsmouth imagining that they would be serving in France, only
to find that their journey was considerably longer: they were, in fact, going to Africa.
What makes this group interesting, then, is that they had little time to prepare, men-
tally or practically, for their encounter with the colonial world. This lack of prepar-
ation offers us potential insight into their developing attitudes toward empire and
imperial concerns. Through their experiences -documented in writing but also
through photography -we learn about their evolving understandings of concepts like
race and colonialism. Unlike enthusiasts or volunteers -such as those who fought in
the South African War -who would have read up on their destination or their
expected duties, these were ordinary men coming to terms with what they saw before
them.
The shock of these men on their arrival in Africa, and the sense of loss, confu-
sion, and chaos that followed, is documented in their letters and diaries. The jour-
ney from port of arrival to place of deployment was generally not straightforward.
In their writings, men often described not being able to find their units, or that
when they discovered these units finding them to be not properly equipped.
Officers travelling by themselves, especially, were not only lost in military bureau-
cracy but also lost in a literal sense as they tried to find both a mode of transport
and the correct route to their destination. One medical officer recalled his sentiment
after arriving in East Africa and being unable to gather any information about his
employment: 'Nobody seemed to worry whether I came or not. I was just a nobody
and [ … ] it wouldn't have mattered if I hadn't arrived at all.' 15 This confusing situ-
ation was rooted in the military nature of this campaign. After years of stalemate,
in 1916 British forces renewed efforts to take control of German territory, only to
be met by a highly mobile defensive campaign by the German Schutztruppe, later
often described as guerrilla-style, which successfully delayed the final surrender
until November 1918. 16 In this period, although large sections of the German col-
ony were under formal Allied occupation, there was also a nearly continuous cam-
paign, which compromised infrastructure and transport routes, forcing troops into
long marches and living in tents with very little equipment.
In addition to its physical challenges, warfare in East Africa was also socially
challenging. While they were coming to terms with being at war, newly arriving
men from Europe also had to come to terms with their position in a racialised colo-
nial hierarchy. 17 This context required them to keep an eye trained on any 'non-
white people' around them and to respond to the role implied by their own
Europeanness, while also being observant of and acting in line with their military
position. The combination of military and social pressures, along with the relative
naivety of those encountering them and the capacity to process novel experiences
text.note: 15 N.S. Bruce, Interview October 1980, Liddle Archive (Leeds), AFE 06.

16 Ross Anderson, The Forgotten Front: The East African Campaign 1914-1918 (Cheltenham: The
History Press, 2014).
17 Steinbach, 'Between Intimacy and Violence', 98-122.
D. STEINBACH
text.body:
not just through words but also photographic imagery, offers much for the histor-
ian of the first world war in East Africa to analyse.
When examining the photographic material produced by these men, two themes
become apparent. One immediately obvious theme follows classic nineteenth cen-
tury military aesthetics in which everything was orderly -both socially and militar-
ily. White soldiers sit in the middle of the frame with African soldiers arranged
around them; equipment flows in an orderly fashion with motor cars and rifles
neatly lined up. Visual imagery therefore conveyed the idea of a 'proper' war. Yet,
behind the visual order a second, less immediately obvious, theme is apparent.
Especially when considered against the challenging and chaotic reality of war in
East Africa, as briefly described above, the images produced by these men seem
compensatory. Behind the order in the foreground, some images also reveal the con-
fusion and contradiction that men were trying to process. I approach the photo-
graphic material through these two lenses.
Many men purchased cameras after they enlisted to document their experience.
As such, for many of these men, taking photographs was a new skill they were
acquiring. As one officer wrote to his niece shortly after arriving in East Africa:
I hope you will like them [the photos], they are not really successful, but as we are
only amateurs we have to learn by experience, and so a little later on, I may be able
to send you something better. 18
Yet, despite their amateur status, the men readily drew on established visual
forms. As such, their photographs did not just capture an immediate and unfiltered
reality that stood before them -instead, images were created through the staging
and positioning of people in specific ways. For example, officers are often sur-
rounded by their troops in a hierarchical formation. This is, of course, a very com-
mon trope of colonial military photography. 19 It is nonetheless noteworthy how
familiar this appeared to officers who had only recently arrived in Africa and who
re-enacted this trope in their own images (Figure 2):
Despite the prevalence of non-Europeans among the forces deployed in East
Africa -predominantly Africans, but also significant numbers of Indians -it is also
noteworthy that relatively few images depict soldiers with their African comrades
in ways that were individualising or spontaneous. White soldiers photographed
themselves with other white soldiers in 'homely' settings but cut out the Africans
that lived with and around them. These were foremost African male servants, gen-
erally referred to as 'boys', who fulfilled domestic tasks like cooking, cleaning,
washing and serving. 20 These servants featured prominently in letters and diaries
where they were described in more detail than fellow African soldiers, but were not
text.note: 18 William Townsend, letter to his niece, 21 December 1914, Liddle Archive (Leeds), AFE 32.

19 Ryan, Picturing empire, 73-98; Christopher Pinney, 'The Prosthetic Eye: Photography as Cure and
Poison', Journal of the Royal Anthropological Institute 14 (2008), 33-46.

20 Moyd, Violent intermediaries; Robyn A. Pariser, 'The Servant Problem: African Servants the Making of
European Domesticity in Colonial Tanganyika', in Towards a Global History of Domestic and
Caregiving Workers, ed. By Dirk Hoerder, Elise van Nederveen Meerkerk, and Silke Neunsinger
(Leiden/Boston: Brill, 2015), 271-95.
PICTURING AFRICA AND DOCUMENTING WAR
text.body:
captured on camera. Instead, one finds staged photographs that displayed a
'natural' hierarchy that did not actually exist in the experiences of men who fre-
quently lamented how difficult it was to exercise power over their 'boys' and
affirming that 'it is an unwritten rule that a white man must on no account allow
himself to be out-willed by a black' (Figure 3). 21
This involved a form of staging that was beyond the individual photos them-
selves and involved the positioning of images together in albums. For example, here
we have a page from photograph album by W. G. Hargrave. One side shows a pic-
ture of two relaxed British officers, dressed in khaki positioned in front of the
African bush. On the other side of the page, a photograph of an African sentry
standing guard next to a hut -saluting into the emptiness. These images taken out
of context and then repositioned together created the desired effect of a racial hier-
archy and the imagination of an imperial officer at ease (Figure 4).
Another example of this can be seen in the above arrangement, found in an
anonymous photo album. The set of images contrasted white officers having
'Breakfast at Marago' while 'on the trek' with an image of African porters 'on the
march'. Though both sets of people were -together -engaged in war, the different
language of their movement is itself striking: one treks, the other marches.
Moreover, the officers depicted in the first image were enjoying a classic colonial
breakfast complete with white tablecloths and cups with saucers. 22 The second
image, other than taking place on the same day, seemed to have little to do with the
previous scene. Placed together they contrasted the casual preparation, relaxed
composure and individual personality of Europeans with the orderliness of a de-
individualised line-up of non-Europeans.
FIGURE 2.
Photo from album by John Hopper (n.d.), Liddle Archive (Leeds), AFE 34.
text.note: 21 Frederick J. Smith, letter to his wife, 8 October 1916, Liddle Archive (Leeds), AFE 29.

22 On colonial food photography: Susie Protschky, 'Tea Cups, Cameras and Family Life: Picturing
Domesticity in Elite European and Javanese Family Photographs from the Netherlands Indies, Ca.
1900-42', History of Photography 36, no. 1 (2012), 44-65.
D. STEINBACH
text.body:
These photographs were of course not veridical snapshots of life in the base camp
or at the front. Instead, they were scenarios that were staged and curated into a
memento of military action and a record of an intact colonial hierarchy. Despite the
serenity of their breakfast, the combination of images reassured the intended viewer
that they were not simply leisurely colonials, but instead men in control of their
bodies, their surroundings and the people they dominated. In their photographs,
ordinary white soldiers recreated this structure en miniature, for example, as in the
image below, by positing themselves in an elevated pose relative to Africans (Figure 5).
Images like the ones presented above were not the kind that entered into the pub-
lic domain. All of these are taken from private albums and likely created for a more
constrained and intimate audience of family and friends -as well as the idea of
themselves as an audience reflecting back on their experiences at some later date.
But, more than other fronts, the press coverage of the East African campaign also
depended on photographs taken by ordinary soldiers. There were some semi-offi-
cial photographers based in the large depots at Nairobi, Mombasa or Dar es
Salaam, but the campaign itself was not systematically documented. Gaps in official
coverage were typically filled by photographs taken by those participants in the
campaign who had both the equipment and the necessary connections to local,
regional or even national newspapers. Generally, these were middle-class officers. 23
As such, the popular perception of the war in East Africa was very much shaped by
the impression of these men and their selection of photographs. Typically, this
FIGURE 3.
Page from photograph album (EA 1915-1917) by W. G. Hargrave, Liddle Archive
(Leeds), AFE 13.
text.note: 23 George A. Pim, letter to his mother, 10 March 1915, Liddle Archive (Leeds), AFE 24.
PICTURING AFRICA AND DOCUMENTING WAR
text.body:
selection stressed two things. On the one hand, images portrayed the 'importance'
of this sideshow campaign, the seriousness of the military engagement, and the sac-
rifices made by the men. On the other hand, images also foregrounded the exoti-
cism of the overall setting.
The pictures from The Illustrated London News, displayed at the beginning of
this article, 24 provide a particularly striking -and exceptional -example of both
the interplay between public and private photography, and between imagery com-
bining the colonial front with the home front. These images were provided by
FIGURE 4.
Anonymous photo album 'Album 3 (GEA 1914-1918)', Archive of SANDF.
text.note: 24 The Illustrated London News 148 (4047), 11 November 1916, 570.
D. STEINBACH
text.body:
Francis Brett Young, a young British doctor and aspiring author who served with
the Royal Army Medical Corps. During his time in East Africa, he not only served
with soldiers from different parts of Africa, but also with different Indian regi-
ments. He took interest and pride in familiarising himself with the different cus-
toms, traditions, and habits of Africans and Indians and recorded these with much
fascination and detail. 25 Serving as an officer with the Rhodesian troops he sent
photographs via his wife to The Illustrated London News. 26 We do not know how
many photographs he sent, but the paper published six of them, all emphasising the
dynamic and forward drive of the campaign: white soldiers -under a looming can-
non -marching, a long row of armoured motorcars, and a train ready to depart.
The Indian soldiers were shown at camp and, of course, the immobile 'enemy pris-
oners under guard' were also depicted. These photos provide a good example of
how text and image could be manipulated -and of the importance of, as much as
possible, locating images in their original sources before interpreting them. In a let-
ter to his wife, Brett Young complained about the descriptions put to his
FIGURE 5.
Photograph from album by Private H. Calderbank (GEA 1916-18), Imperial War
Museum, 8512-27.
text.note:
25 He served initially with the 2nd Rhodesian Regiment, then the Combined Field Ambulance Unit B120
(India Section), which became attached to 130th Baluchis, and finally the 2nd Kashmir Rifles. After
active service he was posted to Nairobi in 1917 where he was put in charge of the Indian General
Hospital and later the Maharajah Scindia of Gwalior Convalescent Home for Officers. He published his
memoirs before the war ended and shaped the image of the campaign: Francis Brett Young, Marching
on Tanga: With General Smuts in East Africa (London: W. Collins, 1917).

26 Francis Brett Young, letter to his wife, 11 November 1916, Cadbury Research Library (Birmingham),
FBY 483.
PICTURING AFRICA AND DOCUMENTING WAR
text.body:
photographs. 27 Other than the image depicting the 130th Baluchis which was 'right
for once', all others were 'mislabelled' by the newspaper. The photos 1 to 4 became
less specific in terms of their location, which Brett Young originally named and
labelled accurately. This could be in response to either censorship or self-censorship
by the newspapers, or it could be a simplification for the sake of readers. The most
striking miscrediting was the photo 'enemy prisoners under guard: a batch of
German-drilled askaris'. This photo, as Brett Young pointed out, actually shows
'friendly natives at Kilimanjaro from whom I bought my beautiful Billi [his pet]'. In
this case, the 'mislabelling' appeared to reflect a desire to depict positive 'results' of
the campaign. These tendencies to mislabel, simplify, and depict results would go
on to shape the public imagining of the war in 'Africa'.
Other than people, their (hierarchical) relationships, and the (exotic) settings in
which war was waged, photographs also depicted a range of important objects.
Here again, in the depiction of objects, we can see some of the same themes emerg-
ing. Together with the railway, 28 one recurring visual icon of the East African cam-
paign was the motorcar. 29 Rows of vehicles parked in order, ready to make the
conquest of German East Africa possible. The orderliness mirrored both the notion
of a military column ready to march and the presence of a reliable force.
Photographs depicted cars crossing rickety bridges, traversing riverbeds and man-
aging potholed roads. Arguably, these images celebrated the knowhow of Western
mechanics and their driving skills. Notably, soldiers did not photograph broken
down and abandoned cars and lorries. These undoubtedly existed in the landscape
around them; as such their absence was not one of limited opportunity. Although it
could be argued that broken down and abandoned cars do not make interesting
photographic subjects, the absence of such objects in degraded states also seems to
underscore the importance of presenting equipment as intact, operational, and
ready for war. Even if the explanation for absence was more banal, it contributed
to a visual body depicting the machinery of war in proper working order.
Also notable by their absence were African drivers, of whom there were no pho-
tographs. 30 Again, since African drivers did exist, their absence could suggest that
they would contradict the preferred narrative of a white man in control of a com-
plex machine overcoming an adverse environment. Or, as one British member of
the Motor Transport unit in Dar es Salaam put it in his memoirs: 'natives are bad
drivers. I only saw one on the road and he, singularly, came to grief before our very
eyes.' 31 One image that came close to contradicting this point portrayed five
text.note:
27 Francis Brett Young, letter to his wife, 28 December 1916, Cadbury Research Library (Birmingham),
FBY 546.

28 Giorgio Miescher, 'Arteries of Empire: On the Geographical Imagination of South Africa's Railway War,
1914/1915', Kronos 38, no. 1 (2012), 22-46.

29 Jan-Bart Gewald, Sabine Luning, and Klaas Van Walraven, 'Motor Vehicles and People in Africa: An
Introduction', in The Speed of Change (Leiden: Brill, 2009), 1-18[AQ3]; Jeanne Van Eeden, 'Picturing
the Road: Automobility in Selected South African Postcards', Communication 38, no. 1 (2012), 84-102.

30 Melvin Page, 'Africa's First "High Tech" War: The Technological Impact of World War One on
Africans', Journal of African Military History 2, no. 1 (2018), 24-61.

31 William Wallace Campbell, East Africa by Motor Lorry: Recollections of an Ex-motor Transport Driver
(London: J. Murray, 1928), 111.
D. STEINBACH
text.body:
African civilians sitting in a car. This image was rare -just as Africans did not drive,
they also did not typically sit in cars, both of which were jobs for a white man. Yet
any potential threat to the preferred narrative was diffused by the label underneath,
which read 'The wild men of Borneo'. This image had -obviously -nothing to do
with Borneo and instead seemed to reference a set of 'freak show' performers
included in P.T. Barnum's travelling exhibitions, popular at the turn of the twentieth
century. 32 As such, the label transformed an otherwise jolly and humanising scene
into something ridiculous and derogatory. This example is a particularly good illus-
tration of the value of combining imagery and text for analysis -in this case the
label completely transformed the meaning of the accompanying image in the later
assembled album (Figure 6).
Orderly images of people and objects -both depicted in their right place and
state -underlined the first theme of depicting both a 'proper war' and proper
'colonialism'. Previously, however, I suggested that behind these images might be
lurking something more, that is, an awareness of the contradictions posed by fight-
ing an European war in a colonial space. Between these two worlds -war and colo-
nialism -there was much for the men to ponder, process and reconcile. For
example, approaching Africa as white men, many soldiers expected their whiteness
to matter somehow. But, when interacting with their comrades, military hierarchies
mattered more, something that positioned many working-class soldiers back at the
bottom. In interacting with Africans, whiteness was surely a signifier of expected
status. But the inexperienced and unprepared soldiers arriving in Africa were also
heavily dependent on locals and their superior knowledge, positioning them again
at the bottom of an informational hierarchy. How did men come to terms with sit-
uations in which their whiteness was not an advantage and did not matter as much
as they perhaps thought it should? Other work has analysed the consequences of
white soldiers' precarious status for their actions towards, for example, 'house
boys' and the balance between intimacy and violence in the domestic sphere.
Although photographic evidence cannot speak to the resolution of undermined sta-
tus at the individual level, the accumulated imagery provides some clues to how the
awkwardness of military and colonial status was processed and re-aligned
collectively.
If navigating social codes at the intersection of military and colonial hierarchies
was awkward, the act of warfare against a fellow colonial power was even more
so. This particular awkwardness is already apparent in the ambivalence of press
and public opinion in the colonies prior to war being declared. It can also be seen
in the visual imagery surrounding battle. The images reproduced above -of
'Breakfast at Marago' and 'Porters on the march' -were taken at the border of
Kenya where the troops were waiting to cross into German East Africa for an
attack. The relaxed mood of the first image undercuts the seriousness -and signifi-
cance -of the battles that were fought here.
text.note:
32 Roslyn Poignant, 'The Making of Professional "Savages": From P. T. Barnum (1883) to the Sunday
Times (1998)', in Photography's Other Histories, ed. by Christopher Pinney and Nicolas Peterson
(Durham: Duke University Press, 2003), 55-84.
PICTURING AFRICA AND DOCUMENTING WAR
text.body:
British soldiers in East Africa might have felt like they were on the periphery of war,
away from the 'main event' of the western front. But, like other Allied troops fighting
against German colonies, they were the only forces actually to conquer German terri-
tory. As such, their campaign was ultimately a victory -and a notable one at that.
Given this, one could expect many images depicting the heroism of warfare and the
triumph of victory over the enemy. Yet, images depicting either battle or the enemy
are largely absent from wartime photographs of Africa. The absence of battle imagery
is understandable -not only is battle very difficult to anticipate but soldiers in battle
typically do not pause to take photographs. Yet, the general absence of the enemy,
and the specificity of the images in which they are portrayed, still seems revealing.
Most often, we see the enemy -that is, Germans -only indirectly. To a certain
extent, this accurately reflects the overall experiences of the campaign, in which sol-
diers rarely saw their enemy directly, that is face-to-face. Instead, photographs
depict things destroyed by Germans. In that sense, Germans themselves are more
akin to 'afterimages'. What we especially see are destroyed symbols of cultural and
technical progress that were brought to Africa by European colonisers. That is,
rather than general scenes of destruction, images depicted destroyed railway lines
and bridges. On the one hand, these images accurately documented the military
retreat of German forces. On the other hand, these images also documented the
destruction of key symbols of colonial progress and of German investment in their
colonies. As such, the images bore witness to the collapse of the German imperial
project to bring economic, technical and cultural progress to Africa. As Francis
Brett Young reported to his wife about 'the utter desolation of the country':
The pulled mealie fields, with never a single head of corn, green plantain groves
without fruit, great hulks of abandoned lorries (many 3 ton Napiers and Daimlers)
FIGURE 6.
Photograph from album by Private H. Calderbank (GEA 1916-18), Imperial War
Museum, 8512-27.
text.note: D. STEINBACH
text.body:
and countless mules and oxen which had not been dragged away from the road,
stinking horribly. [ … ] This miserable panorama of waste was not encouraging. 33
Seen in these terms, images of German destruction gave additional weight to
British troops' own presence in Africa and reinforced the importance of their mis-
sion to occupy German territory. In so doing, they were not just claiming enemy
land, or some distant territory; they were also defending the colonial civilising mis-
sion against an enemy that disregarded these values.
Where we do see the enemy directly, rather than just through their actions, is in
images of German prisoners of war. 34 But these are not very interesting photo-
graphs. They were typically taken from quite far back, with people not appearing as
discernible individuals, but rather as anonymous small dots. The series of images
below, depicting prisoners of war outside the context of battle, is an example of this.
The vagueness of their depiction is notable -for example, we do not clearly see any
individual prisoners waiting to be transported. The differentiation of categories of
prisoners is also revealing. All of these prisoners of war were equally the enemy. Yet,
white prisoners were waiting in cars by which they would be transported, whereas
African prisoners were waiting to be marched up to internment camps. The form
and content of these images therefore revealed something important about the rela-
tion between the British and Germans in this particular theatre of war -as fellow
Europeans, German prisoners were treated differently from Africans (Figure 7).
As has been examined elsewhere, the reality of German prisoners of war in
Africa was confronting to the colonial racial order -an order in which Europeans
should not be fighting against each other and with the support of Africans. 35
Indeed, every British unit had a political officer from the colonial office attached to
the military command to make sure that when an area was conquered, or prisoners
of war were taken, that the white Germans were not humiliated and that there
was no improper behaviour like looting or wild drinking by the conquering
forces. 36 Images like the ones above further reveal the care and attention given to
preserving the dignity of German prisoners of war, for example by separating them
and transporting them in comfort to their eventual internment. Seen in this way,
the images are also reflective of the more general desire of occupying forces to strike

during the First World War', in Other Combatants, Other Fronts: Competing Histories of the First

PICTURING AFRICA AND DOCUMENTING WAR
text.body:
a balance between taking over the colony without simultaneously upsetting or dis-
crediting European colonial rule.
This desire to strike a balance between the objectives of war and colonialism can
be seen in further examples. German colonial rule and national identity were par-
ticularly embodied in statues of the former German chancellor Otto von Bismarck,
the Kaiser and several colonial heroes, which were erected in the decade before the
war in the central squares of nearly all larger towns in the colony. 37 One might
expect that these would be obvious targets for occupying troops. Even though the
approaching British troops did deface the statue of Hermann von Wissmann in Dar
es Salaam with white paint, there were no official steps undertaken to cover up or
remove the statue following this (Figures 8 and 9).
In preserving colonial ideals, even in the treatment of enemy prisoners and sym-
bols, this very complex and brutal campaign was re-worked into a simplified famil-
iar narrative: strong white men conquered nature, conquered people, and defeated
their adversaries. Indeed, it was the African landscape that recurred most regularly
in photographs -a landscape that was generally empty of any human presence, nei-
ther African civilian nor African troops, let alone any Germans.
An overarching narrative of the East African campaign as being 'a gentleman's
war' developed through the interwar years. This sanitised version of the conflict was
FIGURE 7.
Anonymous photo album, 'Album 9 (East Africa 1917/18)', Archive of SANDF.
text.note:
37 Joachim Zeller, Kolonialdenkm€ aler und Geschichtsbewußtsein. Eine Untersuchung der kolonialdeut-
schen Erinnerungskultur (FrankfurtMain: IKO, 2000).
D. STEINBACH
text.body:
useful to both sides. 38 To the Germans, it smoothed their re-entry into the realm of
good Europeans. To the British, it allowed them to omit the support they received
from Indians and Africans from their own narrative. In this narrative, the important
contributions made by troops and labourers from across the British Empire were
completely omitted -contributions that continued to be omitted in subsequent
memoirs and later films and novels depicting the first world war in East Africa.
In the space between the war as it occurred and its subsequent memory, photo-
graphs become an important resource. Read alongside the more explicit reflections
and recollections of soldiers and officers given in their diaries and letters from the
time, photographs provide an opportunity to reinvestigate, reinterpret, and chal-
lenge the roots of the narrative that has subsequently evolved. Although photo-
graphs may have been staged, simplified and mislabelled, these images still capture
some 'reality' of war in this particular place. Photographs especially document the
multi-ethnic, multi-national, and racial aspects of this war, and in so doing bring
back into view some of the contributions made by colonised people to the war
effort. As argued here, photographs are also revealing of the tensions that con-
fronted individual soldiers who found themselves in Africa 'by accident', and by
the wider cultural tensions created by inter-European warfare conducted in the
colonial sphere. Certainly, the content and form -what is (and is not)

Documents.10049.

38 Eckard Michels, 'Der Held Von Deutsch-Ostafrika' Paul Von Lettow-Vorbeck: Ein Preußischer
Kolonialoffizier (Paderborn: Sch€ oningh, 2008), 306-10.
PICTURING AFRICA AND DOCUMENTING WAR
text.body:
photographed and how -provide many examples of common tropes from colonial
photography, war photography, and, perhaps more interestingly, where these things
intersect. Yet, photography as a source also has its limits.
Conclusion
The unexpected deployment of British soldiers to East Africa during the latter half
of the first world war provides an unique window into how European eyes encoun-
tered Africa, and how their vision was shaped by prevailing imperial aesthetics and
popular anthropological ideas. The photographs taken by these soldiers not only
reflect their personal encounters with the continent's landscapes and peoples but
also serve as poignant evidence of the destruction wrought by war -challenging the
myth of the 'civilising mission' that underpinned colonial ideology. The soldiers'
roles as both combatants and unintentional tourists complicates our understanding
of their experiences, and deeper analysis of the content and staging of their photo-
graphs highlights a complex interplay between idealised perceptions and not always
compliant realties. By capturing images of both beauty and devastation, these men
documented a crucial moment of colonial history that speaks to the broader impli-
cations of imperialism and global war, while also crafting visual narratives that
influenced public understandings and resonated through post-colonial discourse.

Notes on contributor
Daniel Steinbach is associate professor of European colonial history at the
University of Copenhagen. He works on the global dimension of the First World
War with a particular interest in the interaction between African, Indian, and
European soldiers and civilians in the colonial theatres of war and the representation
and memory of these campaigns in Europe and Africa. He co-edited Colonial
Encounters in a Time of Global Conflict, 1914-1918 (London: Routledge, 2021).
